Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Code Correctness in LLMs via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally represent and process code correctness? The paper applies sparse autoencoders to identify and analyze directions in model representations that correspond to code correctness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses sparse autoencoders to identify and analyze code correctness directions in LLMs, revealing that error detection is reliable but correction via steering involves tradeoffs, and that these mechanisms persist from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify code correctness directions in LLMs, revealing mechanistic insights that have practical applications for prompting and error detection.
papers.key_findings:
Detection directions predict errors reliably (F1: 0.821) but fail as confidence indicators for correct code (F1: 0.504).
Steering interventions produce significant corrections but introduce tradeoffs, fixing 4.04% of errors but corrupting 14.66% of correct code.
Attention analysis shows test cases matter more than problem descriptions for successful code generation.
Weight orthogonalization proves correct directions are necessary for generation, their removal causing 83.62% corruption.
Code correctness features persist from base to chat models, with directions from base Gemma-2 retaining effectiveness after instruction-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The correct-predicting feature has low precision (0.362) due to false positives, limiting its utility as a confidence indicator.
Steering interventions correct only 4.04% of errors while corrupting 14.66% of correct code, indicating a tradeoff.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models become integral to software development, with substantial portions of AI-suggested code entering production, understanding their internal correctness mechanisms becomes critical for safe deployment. We apply sparse autoencoders to decompose LLM representations, identifying directions that correspond to code correctness. We select predictor directions using t-statistics and steering directions through separation scores from base model representations, then analyze their mechanistic properties through steering, attention analysis, and weight orthogonalization. We find that code correctness directions in LLMs reliably predict incorrect code, while correction capabilities, though statistically significant, involve tradeoffs between fixing errors and preserving correct code. Mechanistically, successful code generation depends on attending to test cases rather than problem descriptions. Moreover, directions identified in base models retain their effectiveness after instruction-tuning, suggesting code correctness mechanisms learned during pre-training are repurposed during fine-tuning. Our mechanistic insights suggest three practical applications: prompting strategies should prioritize test examples over elaborate problem descriptions, predictor directions can serve as error alarms for developer review, and these same predictors can guide selective steering, intervening only when errors are anticipated to prevent the code corruption from constant steering.

papers.title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the computational circuits in protein language models that underlie their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoMech, a framework using cross-layer transcoders to discover computational circuits in protein language models, achieving high performance recovery and enabling protein design.
papers.conclusion: ProtoMech establishes a principled framework for protein circuit tracing, revealing interpretable computational pathways and enabling effective protein design.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original ESM2 performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks.
ProtoMech identifies compact circuits using <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.
Steering along the discovered circuits enables high-fitness protein design, outperforming baseline methods in more than 70% of cases.
The circuits correspond to known structural and functional motifs, such as binding sites and catalytic loops.
ProtoMech provides a more accurate approximation of ESM2's computation than per-layer transcoder baselines.
papers.limitation: Full replacement models, where both attention and MLP computations are replaced, lead to substantial performance degradation due to compounding reconstruction errors.
future_direction: Developing robust full replacement models remains an active area of research.
Using a tanh loss for constraining sparsity is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model's full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

papers.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to interpret the internal representations of a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model (MAIRA-2) and steer its generations?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology MLLM MAIRA-2, identifying a subset of interpretable clinical concepts within its representations and demonstrating the feasibility and challenges of steering model generations using these features.
papers.conclusion: The study provides initial insights into the internal concepts of MAIRA-2 using SAEs, marking a step toward mechanistic interpretability, while highlighting practical and methodological challenges in automated interpretability and steering.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset (1.8%) of SAE features are highly interpretable (F1 > 0.75), corresponding to clinically relevant concepts like medical devices, pathologies, and textual features.
Nearly half (46%) of SAE features are not interpretable by the automated pipeline (F1 < 0.5).
Steering model generations using SAE features is possible but produces more off-target changes than on-target changes, with success highly dependent on the specific feature.
There is a strong correlation between the on-target effects of positive and negative steering coefficients.
The trained SAEs and their automated interpretations are publicly released to foster further research.
papers.limitation:
Many SAE features (46%) are not interpretable by the automated pipeline.
Steering often produces more off-target changes than on-target changes.
The study reveals practical and methodological challenges across the SAE training, automated concept discovery, and steering pipeline.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can improve the safety, transparency and trust of AI models, which is especially important in healthcare applications where decisions often carry significant consequences. Mechanistic interpretability, particularly through the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs), offers a promising approach for uncovering human-interpretable features within large transformer-based models. In this study, we apply Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology-specialised multimodal large language model, MAIRA-2, to interpret its internal representations. Using large-scale automated interpretability of the SAE features, we identify a range of clinically relevant concepts - including medical devices (e.g., line and tube placements, pacemaker presence), pathologies such as pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, longitudinal changes and textual features. We further examine the influence of these features on model behaviour through steering, demonstrating directional control over generations with mixed success. Our results reveal practical and methodological challenges, yet they offer initial insights into the internal concepts learned by MAIRA-2 - marking a step toward deeper mechanistic understanding and interpretability of a radiology-adapted multimodal large language model, and paving the way for improved model transparency. We release the trained SAEs and interpretations: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/maira-2-sae.

papers.title: CRISP: Persistent Concept Unlearning via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to achieve persistent concept unlearning in large language models using sparse autoencoders to remove harmful knowledge while maintaining model utility.
papers.core_contribution: CRISP is a parameter-efficient method for persistent concept unlearning in LLMs using sparse autoencoders, achieving state-of-the-art performance by selectively suppressing harmful features while preserving benign knowledge and fluency.
papers.conclusion: CRISP is an effective sparse autoencoder-based method for persistent unlearning in LLMs, offering improved performance and interpretability through feature-level suppression.
papers.key_findings:
CRISP outperforms prior methods like ELM and RMU on WMDP benchmarks, with higher overall scores.
It maintains better fluency and concept scores after unlearning, as shown in qualitative and quantitative evaluations.
Feature analysis reveals that CRISP identifies semantically coherent target features for suppression, enabling precise unlearning.
CRISP demonstrates a superior trade-off between unlearning efficacy and retention of benign knowledge.
The method is effective across different models, including Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B.
papers.limitation:
Relies on pretrained SAEs, and effectiveness may diminish if SAEs fail to capture disentangled or interpretable features.
Evaluation is limited to safety-critical domains, and generalization to new tasks and domains is not yet understood.
No formal theoretical guarantees of complete knowledge removal; residual information may persist, and robustness against adversarial extraction is an open direction.
future_direction: Robustness against adversarial extraction
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the need to selectively remove unwanted knowledge while preserving model utility has become paramount. Recent work has explored sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to perform precise interventions on monosemantic features. However, most SAE-based methods operate at inference time, which does not create persistent changes in the model's parameters. Such interventions can be bypassed or reversed by malicious actors with parameter access. We introduce CRISP, a parameter-efficient method for persistent concept unlearning using SAEs. CRISP automatically identifies salient SAE features across multiple layers and suppresses their activations. We experiment with two LLMs and show that our method outperforms prior approaches on safety-critical unlearning tasks from the WMDP benchmark, successfully removing harmful knowledge while preserving general and in-domain capabilities. Feature-level analysis reveals that CRISP achieves semantically coherent separation between target and benign concepts, allowing precise suppression of the target features.

papers.title: Probing the Representational Power of Sparse Autoencoders in Vision Models
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting and steering vision models, and do they provide semantically meaningful features across different vision architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs extract semantically meaningful features from vision models, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable semantic steering in diffusion models, establishing SAEs as a valuable interpretability tool for vision.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are semantically meaningful and enhance interpretable understanding across vision encoders, multimodal LLMs, and diffusion models, highlighting SAEs as a unified interpretability tool across diverse vision architectures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features from vision encoders improve out-of-distribution generalization compared to original embeddings.
SAE features capture hierarchical semantic structures (ontological features) in image encoders.
SAEs enable semantic steering in diffusion models by manipulating text encoder features.
SAEs reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities in LMMs.
Different SAE variants (ReLU, TopK, Gated) show similar trends in reconstruction and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Findings on multimodal representation overlap in LMMs are preliminary and require future quantitative validation.
Steering Stable Diffusion 3.5 is more challenging due to its complex text encoding architecture.
future_direction: Quantitative validation of multimodal representation overlap in LMMs.
Systematic investigation of how visual representations evolve through LLM layers.
Future application of SAEs in vision models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a popular tool for interpreting the hidden states of large language models (LLMs). By learning to reconstruct activations from a sparse bottleneck layer, SAEs discover interpretable features from the high-dimensional internal representations of LLMs. Despite their popularity with language models, SAEs remain understudied in the visual domain. In this work, we provide an extensive evaluation the representational power of SAEs for vision models using a broad range of image-based tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that SAE features are semantically meaningful, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable controllable generation across three vision model architectures: vision embedding models, multi-modal LMMs and diffusion models. In vision embedding models, we find that learned SAE features can be used for OOD detection and provide evidence that they recover the ontological structure of the underlying model. For diffusion models, we demonstrate that SAEs enable semantic steering through text encoder manipulation and develop an automated pipeline for discovering human-interpretable attributes. Finally, we conduct exploratory experiments on multi-modal LLMs, finding evidence that SAE features reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities. Our study provides a foundation for SAE evaluation in vision models, highlighting their strong potential improving interpretability, generalization, and steerability in the visual domain.

papers.title: Beyond Input Activations: Identifying Influential Latents by Gradient Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Do all activated latents in a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) contribute equally to the model's output, and are only latents with high causal influence effective for model steering?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes GradSAE, a method that uses output-side gradient information to identify the most causally influential latents in Sparse Autoencoders, enabling more accurate interpretation and effective steering of LLM behavior.
papers.conclusion: GradSAE effectively identifies influential latents in SAEs and enables more reliable model steering, with results generalizing across different SAEs and layers.
papers.key_findings:
Not all activated SAE latents contribute equally to the model's output; only a subset has high causal influence.
GradSAE more accurately identifies influential latents compared to a baseline that uses only input activations.
Latents selected by GradSAE are more effective for steering the model's output in a local steering task.
The performance gap between masking top and bottom influential latents is consistent across different model layers and SAEs.
Modifying non-influential (BottomK) latents has negligible impact on model output.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on SAEs trained on instruction-tuned LLMs and one fundamental capability (instruction following for question answering). Extending GradSAE to a broader range of scenarios, including pre-trained LLMs, is noted as future work.
future_direction: Extending GradSAE to a broader range of scenarios, including pre-trained LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as powerful tools for interpreting and steering the internal representations of large language models (LLMs). However, conventional approaches to analyzing SAEs typically rely solely on input-side activations, without considering the causal influence between each latent feature and the model's output. This work is built on two key hypotheses: (1) activated latents do not contribute equally to the construction of the model's output, and (2) only latents with high causal influence are effective for model steering. To validate these hypotheses, we propose Gradient Sparse Autoencoder (GradSAE), a simple yet effective method that identifies the most influential latents by incorporating output-side gradient information.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Steering Effectiveness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the reliability of activation-based steering in LLMs be diagnosed using internal model signals such as entropy and KL divergence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that internal mechanistic signals (NBF and KL divergence) can predict steering effectiveness and introduces rotation-based steering as a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods.
papers.conclusion: Internal mechanistic signals can predict steering effectiveness, and rotation-based steering provides a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods, making steering a more measurable and predictable process.
papers.key_findings:
LLM judges (ChatGPT-4o-mini and Gemini-Flash-2.5) show substantial agreement in evaluating steering outputs after correcting for calibration bias.
Effective steering is characterized by structured entropy preservation (NBF) and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps.
Internal signals (NBF, KL, attention patterns) can predict steering quality with reasonable accuracy.
Rotation-based steering outperforms naive additive steering in terms of steering-coherence trade-off.
Attention patterns show a drop in confidence immediately after the intervention layer, correlating with coherence.
papers.limitation:
Limited conceptual coverage (only nine target concepts).
Focus on GEMMA model family, may not generalize to newer models.
Regression formulation requires further refinement.
Label noise from LLM-based judges and qualitative nature of tasks.
papers.abstract: Activation-based steering enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to exhibit targeted behaviors by intervening on intermediate activations without retraining. Despite its widespread use, the mechanistic factors that govern when steering succeeds or fails remain poorly understood, as prior work has relied primarily on black-box outputs or LLM-based judges. In this study, we investigate whether the reliability of steering can be diagnosed using internal model signals. We focus on two information-theoretic measures: the entropy-derived Normalized Branching Factor (NBF), and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between steered activations and targeted concepts in the vocabulary space. We hypothesize that effective steering corresponds to structured entropy preservation and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps. Building on a reliability study demonstrating high inter-judge agreement between two architecturally distinct LLMs, we use LLM-generated annotations as ground truth and show that these mechanistic signals provide meaningful predictive power for identifying successful steering and estimating failure probability. We further introduce a stronger evaluation baseline for Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-based steering, the two most widely adopted activation-steering methods.

papers.title: LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we precisely identify and modify latent feature representations to improve the semantic consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) when responding to semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LF-Steering, a novel activation steering method that uses a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to decompose transformer layer hidden states into a sparsely activated, higher-dimensional feature space, enabling precise identification and adjustment of features responsible for semantic inconsistency to improve LLM performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LF-Steering method effectively enhances the semantic consistency of LLMs by enabling precise, feature-level activation steering, leading to significant task performance gains across a range of NLU and NLG datasets.
papers.key_findings:
LF-Steering achieves state-of-the-art performance in enhancing semantic consistency, outperforming baseline activation steering methods on NLU and NLG tasks.
Feature-level steering using SAE features significantly outperforms neuron-level (hidden state) steering, demonstrating the advantage of operating on decoupled feature representations.
The method shows good locality, not negatively impacting performance on out-of-domain datasets and sometimes improving it.
Middle to final transformer layers (layers 17-32 in LLama2-7B-Chat) are most significantly associated with semantic inconsistency.
The effectiveness of the method depends on selecting appropriate hyperparameters, such as the feature difference threshold and steering strength.
papers.limitation: Addressing semantic inconsistency at a single transformer layer may offer only a partial solution, as relevant latent representations may span multiple layers.
future_direction: Focus on identifying and steering circuits across multiple transformer layers to enhance the LLM's semantic consistency.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate inconsistent responses when prompted with semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs. Recently, activation steering, a technique that modulates LLMs' behaviours by adjusting their latent representations during inference time, has been explored to improve the semantic consistency of LLMs. However, these methods typically operate at the model component level, such as layer hidden states or attention head outputs. They face a challenge due to the ``polysemanticity issue'', where the model components of LLMs typically encode multiple entangled features, making precise steering difficult. To address this challenge, we drill down to feature-level representations and propose LF-Steering, a novel activation steering approach to precisely identify latent feature representations responsible for semantic inconsistency. More specifically, our method maps the hidden states of the relevant transformer layer into a sparsely activated, high-dimensional feature space based on a sparse autoencoder (SAE), ensuring model steering based on decoupled feature representations with minimal interference. Comprehensive experiments on NLU and NLG datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in enhancing semantic consistency, resulting in significant performance gains for various NLU and NLG tasks.

papers.title: Causal Language Control in Multilingual Transformers via Sparse Feature Steering
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoder (SAE) features be leveraged to steer the generated language of multilingual LLMs during inference without fine-tuning or explicit prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for causal language control in multilingual transformers by steering sparse autoencoder features, showing high success rates and layer-specific effectiveness.
papers.conclusion: Demonstrates that SAE features can be causally steered for controlled language shifts, revealing layer-localized sensitivity and architectural mechanisms like attention head specialization.
papers.key_findings:
Steering a single SAE feature can shift output language with up to 90% success while preserving semantic fidelity.
Language steering is most effective in mid-to-late transformer layers.
Specific attention heads, such as Head 12 in Layer 29, amplify language-sensitive SAE features.
Steering performance varies across layers and languages, with some layers showing localized attention contributions and others relying on inherited features.
The method outperforms prompt-based baselines in language classification accuracy for some languages.
papers.limitation:
All experiments are conducted exclusively on the Gemma model family, limiting generalizability to other architectures.
Identification of language-divergent SAE features relies on a fixed dataset of parallel sentences, which may not capture full diversity.
Evaluation depends on automatic metrics (FastText and LaBSE), which do not fully reflect human judgments of fluency or meaning preservation.
SAE features are derived from a pretrained sparse autoencoder and are not learned end-to-end for the steering task, limiting optimality.
Computational requirements are nontrivial for inference and scaling to larger models.
future_direction: Generalizing the framework to non-language attributes (e.g., tone, dialect)
Extending interpretability analysis to MLP contributions and other model families
papers.abstract: Deterministically controlling the target generation language of large multilingual language models (LLMs) remains a fundamental challenge, particularly in zero-shot settings where neither explicit language prompts nor fine-tuning are available. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, previously shown to correlate with interpretable model behaviors, can be leveraged to steer the generated language of LLMs during inference. Leveraging pretrained SAEs on the residual streams of Gemma-2B and Gemma-9B, we identify features whose activations differ most significantly between English and four target languages: Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, and French. By modifying just a single SAE feature at one transformer layer, we achieve controlled language shifts with up to 90\% success, as measured by FastText language classification, while preserving semantic fidelity according to LaBSE (Language-Agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding) similarity. Our analysis reveals that language steering is most effective in mid-to-late transformer layers and is amplified by specific attention heads disproportionately associated with language-sensitive SAE features. These results demonstrate the promise of sparse feature steering as a lightweight and interpretable mechanism for controllable multilingual generation.

papers.title: A Survey on Sparse Autoencoders: Interpreting the Internal Mechanisms of Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models. It covers technical frameworks, explanation methods, evaluation metrics, and applications.
papers.limitation:
Incomplete Concept Dictionary
Lack Theoretical Foundations
Reconstruction Errors
Computational Burden
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. Recently, mechanistic interpretability has attracted significant attention from the research community as a means to understand the inner workings of LLMs. Among various mechanistic interpretability approaches, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method due to their ability to disentangle the complex, superimposed features within LLMs into more interpretable components. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of SAEs for interpreting and understanding the internal workings of LLMs. Our major contributions include: (1) exploring the technical framework of SAEs, covering basic architecture, design improvements, and effective training strategies; (2) examining different approaches to explaining SAE features, categorized into input-based and output-based explanation methods; (3) discussing evaluation methods for assessing SAE performance, covering both structural and functional metrics; and (4) investigating real-world applications of SAEs in understanding and manipulating LLM behaviors.

papers.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the amortisation gap in sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and can more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that sparse autoencoder (SAE) encoders are inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference due to an amortisation gap, and demonstrates empirically that more expressive encoders (like MLPs) and sparse coding methods can outperform SAEs, leading to more interpretable features in large language models.
papers.conclusion: More sophisticated sparse inference methods, such as MLPs and sparse coding, can outperform traditional SAE encoders, reducing the amortisation gap and improving interpretability, which opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAE encoders have a provable amortisation gap, making them suboptimal for sparse inference even in solvable cases.
Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and sparse coding consistently outperform SAEs in recovering sparse codes, with sparse coding achieving the highest performance.
The performance advantage of more sophisticated methods is more pronounced in regimes where compressed sensing theory predicts recoverability.
These findings generalize to real-world applications, as shown by training on GPT-2 activations where MLPs yield more interpretable features than SAEs.
The amortisation gap can be reduced with increased compute, with MLPs surpassing SAE performance after a consistent computational threshold.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result on SAE suboptimality is proven for a specific setting (linear-nonlinear encoder, sparse signals in union of subspaces) and may not cover all practical SAE implementations.
future_direction: Pitting optimised sparse coding approaches (e.g., Least Angle Regression, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) against optimised SAE architectures.
Further exploration of top-k sparse coding with proper hyperparameter tuning to achieve Pareto improvements.
Scaling the methods to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work has shown promise in using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable features in neural network representations. However, the simple linear-nonlinear encoding mechanism in SAEs limits their ability to perform accurate sparse inference. Using compressed sensing theory, we prove that an SAE encoder is inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference, even in solvable cases. We then decouple encoding and decoding processes to empirically explore conditions where more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders. Our results reveal substantial performance gains with minimal compute increases in correct inference of sparse codes. We demonstrate this generalises to SAEs applied to large language models, where more expressive encoders achieve greater interpretability. This work opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations and analysing large language model activations.

papers.title: Temporal Sparse Autoencoders: Leveraging the Sequential Nature of Language for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate temporal consistency into sparse autoencoders to better recover high-level semantic features in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs) that incorporate a temporal contrastive loss to encourage consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens, leading to better disentanglement of semantic and syntactic features in language models.
papers.conclusion: Temporal SAEs leverage the sequential nature of language to better extract semantic features, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.
papers.key_findings:
T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
T-SAEs exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal.
T-SAEs show improved disentanglement between high-level (semantic) and low-level (syntactic) features.
T-SAEs provide practical interpretability benefits, such as in safety monitoring and steering.
papers.abstract: Translating the internal representations and computations of models into concepts that humans can understand is a key goal of interpretability. While recent dictionary learning methods such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising route to discover human-interpretable features, they suffer from a variety of problems, including a systematic failure to capture the rich conceptual information that drives linguistic understanding. Instead, they exhibit a bias towards shallow, token-specific, or noisy features, such as "the phrase 'The' at the start of sentences". In this work, we propose that this is due to a fundamental issue with how dictionary learning methods for LLMs are trained. Language itself has a rich, well-studied structure spanning syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; however, current unsupervised methods largely ignore this linguistic knowledge, leading to poor feature discovery that favors superficial patterns over meaningful concepts. We focus on a simple but important aspect of language: semantic content has long-range dependencies and tends to be smooth over a sequence, whereas syntactic information is much more local. Building on this insight, we introduce Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs), which incorporate a novel contrastive loss encouraging consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens. This simple yet powerful modification enables SAEs to disentangle semantic from syntactic features in a self-supervised manner. Across multiple datasets and models, T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Strikingly, they exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.

papers.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the extent of feature space universality across large language models? Specifically, whether SAE feature spaces are similar under rotation-invariant transformations.
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that SAE feature spaces are similar across different LLMs, supporting the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which enables the transfer of interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that feature spaces are universal across LLMs, providing evidence for the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which can facilitate the transfer of interpretability techniques like steering vectors.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of LLMs show the highest similarity in SAE feature spaces, while layer 0 has low similarity.
Semantically meaningful subspaces, such as those for emotions or time, exhibit notable similarity across models.
The similarity is statistically significant as measured by SVCCA and RSA, with p-values below 0.05 for most layer pairs.
The approach works across various model pairs, including Pythia, Gemma, and Llama models.
Filtering non-concept features and many-to-1 mappings improves similarity scores.
papers.abstract: The Universality Hypothesis in large language models (LLMs) claims that different models converge towards similar concept representations in their latent spaces. Providing evidence for this hypothesis would enable researchers to exploit universal properties, facilitating the generalization of mechanistic interpretability techniques across models. Previous works studied if LLMs learned the same features, which are internal representations that activate on specific concepts. Since comparing features across LLMs is challenging due to polysemanticity, in which LLM neurons often correspond to multiple unrelated features rather than to distinct concepts, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been employed to disentangle LLM neurons into SAE features corresponding to distinct concepts. In this paper, we introduce a new variation of the universality hypothesis called Analogous Feature Universality: we hypothesize that even if SAEs across different models learn different feature representations, the spaces spanned by SAE features are similar, such that one SAE space is similar to another SAE space under rotation-invariant transformations. Evidence for this hypothesis would imply that interpretability techniques related to latent spaces, such as steering vectors, may be transferred across models via certain transformations. To investigate this hypothesis, we first pair SAE features across different models via activation correlation, and then measure spatial relation similarities between paired features via representational similarity measures, which transform spaces into representations that reveal hidden relational similarities. Our experiments demonstrate high similarities for SAE feature spaces across various LLMs, providing evidence for feature space universality.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can we identify functionally important features in neural networks? The paper investigates whether standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) learn features that are functionally important for network performance and proposes a new training method to ensure the features are functionally important.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces end-to-end sparse dictionary learning, a method for training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that ensures the learned features are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted.
papers.conclusion: End-to-end sparse dictionary learning offers a Pareto improvement over standard SAEs, requiring fewer features to explain network performance without sacrificing interpretability, bringing us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately.
papers.key_findings:
For the same level of performance explained, end-to-end SAEs require activating more than twice as few features per datapoint compared to standard SAEs.
End-to-end SAEs require fewer total features over the dataset to explain the same amount of network performance.
End-to-end SAEs with downstream reconstruction loss (SAEe2e+ds) achieve similar performance to SAEe2e while having activations that follow more similar pathways through the network compared to the original model.
The improved efficiency of end-to-end SAEs does not come at the cost of interpretability, as measured by automated interpretability scores and qualitative analysis.
End-to-end SAEs have more orthogonal features and are less prone to feature splitting compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation:
End-to-end SAEs take 2-3.5 times longer to train than standard SAEs.
There is a risk that SAEe2e may take different computational pathways through the network, though this is addressed by SAEe2e+ds.
The automated interpretability score is an imperfect metric of interpretability.
future_direction: Using training tweaks such as a sparsity schedule to allow for higher learning rates.
Using locally trained SAEs as initializations to reduce training time.
Training multiple SAEs at different layers concurrently to reduce training time.
papers.abstract: Identifying the features learned by neural networks is a core challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse, overcomplete dictionary that reconstructs a network's internal activations, have been used to identify these features. However, SAEs may learn more about the structure of the datatset than the computational structure of the network. There is therefore only indirect reason to believe that the directions found in these dictionaries are functionally important to the network. We propose end-to-end (e2e) sparse dictionary learning, a method for training SAEs that ensures the features learned are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted. Compared to standard SAEs, e2e SAEs offer a Pareto improvement: They explain more network performance, require fewer total features, and require fewer simultaneously active features per datapoint, all with no cost to interpretability. We explore geometric and qualitative differences between e2e SAE features and standard SAE features. E2e dictionary learning brings us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately. We release our library for training e2e SAEs and reproducing our analysis at https://github.com/ApolloResearch/e2e_sae

papers.title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: Robust Behavior Control in LLMs via Steering Target Atoms
papers.research_question: How can we achieve precise control over language model generation by isolating and manipulating disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Steering Target Atoms (STA), a method that uses SAE-decoupled representations to identify and manipulate target atoms for precise behavior control in LLMs, demonstrating improved safety and robustness over prompt engineering and other steering methods.
papers.conclusion: STA provides a novel method for precise behavior control in LLMs, offering superior robustness and flexibility compared to prompt engineering, and can be extended to control reasoning in large reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
STA achieves state-of-the-art detoxification performance on safety benchmarks, with minimal side effects on general capabilities.
Steering strategies (including STA) are more robust and flexible than prompt engineering, especially in adversarial scenarios.
Steering vectors remain effective even with very few instances (as few as 4).
Steering can control the length of chain-of-thought reasoning in large reasoning models, mitigating overthinking.
Steering in intermediate layers (layers 24-25) is more effective for behavior control.
papers.limitation:
SAE-based methods can be outperformed by simple baselines in some steering tasks, and STA shows limited effectiveness in the personality domain.
Experiments are limited to Gemma and Llama models due to limited public SAE availability.
The study focuses on safety and personality domains; applicability to other domains like multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning is not validated.
future_direction: Extend STA to a broader range of LLMs, including larger and more diverse architectures.
Validate STA in other nuanced domains such as multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning tasks.
Further investigate the performance divergence of SAE-based methods in different domains.
papers.abstract: Precise control over language model generation is vital for ensuring both safety and reliability. Although prompt engineering and steering are commonly used to intervene in model behaviors, the vast number of parameters in models often results in highly intertwined internal representations. This interdependency can limit control precision and sometimes lead to unintended side effects. Recent research has explored the use of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to disentangle knowledge in high-dimensional spaces for steering. However, these applications have been limited to toy tasks owing to the nontrivial issue of locating atomic knowledge components. In this paper, we propose Steering Target Atoms (STA), a novel method that isolates and manipulates disentangled knowledge components to enhance safety. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Further analysis reveals that steering exhibits superior robustness and flexibility, particularly in adversarial scenarios. We also apply the steering strategy to the large reasoning model, confirming its effectiveness in precise reasoning control.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we align Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features with human-defined concepts to create an interpretable and controllable interface for Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: ALIGNSAE is a method that aligns Sparse Autoencoder features with a predefined ontology through a two-stage training curriculum, enabling precise concept-level inspection and control in frozen LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ALIGNSAE provides a verifiable and controllable interface for concept-level manipulation in LLMs, advancing interpretability and steering capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ALIGNSAE achieves near-perfect concept-slot binding in mid-layers (e.g., layer 6) of GPT-2, with diagonal accuracy up to 1.00.
It significantly reduces concept fragmentation and increases top-1 concentration compared to traditional unsupervised SAEs.
Swap interventions demonstrate reliable controllability with a clear fidelity-strength tradeoff, achieving up to 0.847 swap success at layer 6.
In 2-hop reasoning, ALIGNSAE attains 4× higher swap success than traditional SAE.
The method provides mechanistic insights into grokking-like generalization dynamics via step-wise concept binding.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on a limited ontology (6 relations for 1-hop, 20 for 2-hop) and on GPT-2, a relatively small model, which may not reflect performance on larger models or more complex ontologies.
Swap controllability has a narrow effective amplification range (around α=2), and over-amplification can destabilize interventions.
future_direction: Extending ALIGNSAE to larger ontologies and more complex concept types.
Applying the method to larger language models and more diverse tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

papers.title: PolySAE: Modeling Feature Interactions in Sparse Autoencoders via Polynomial Decoding
papers.research_question: How can we extend sparse autoencoders to model non-linear feature interactions (compositional structure) while preserving a linear encoder for interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PolySAE, a sparse autoencoder that extends the decoder with quadratic and cubic terms to model feature interactions via low-rank tensor factorization, improving feature separation and probing performance while maintaining reconstruction fidelity.
papers.conclusion: PolySAE effectively models feature interactions in sparse autoencoders, capturing compositional structure beyond linear combinations and improving interpretability without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
papers.key_findings:
PolySAE achieves an average improvement of approximately 8% in probing F1 across four language models and three SAE variants while maintaining comparable reconstruction error.
PolySAE produces 2–10× larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions, indicating more separated semantic structure.
Learned interaction weights exhibit negligible correlation with co-occurrence frequency (r=0.06), suggesting they capture compositional structure rather than surface statistics.
PolySAE adds a small parameter overhead (3% for GPT-2 small) through low-rank factorization of interaction terms.
Qualitative analysis shows PolySAE captures compositional structures like morphological binding (e.g., 'administrators') and phrasal composition (e.g., 'Starbucks').
papers.limitation: The study is limited to models up to 2B parameters and experiments are restricted to forced-sparsity SAE variants.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method for interpreting neural network representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of dictionary atoms. However, SAEs assume that features combine additively through linear reconstruction, an assumption that cannot capture compositional structure: linear models cannot distinguish whether "Starbucks" arises from the composition of "star" and "coffee" features or merely their co-occurrence. This forces SAEs to allocate monolithic features for compound concepts rather than decomposing them into interpretable constituents. We introduce PolySAE, which extends the SAE decoder with higher-order terms to model feature interactions while preserving the linear encoder essential for interpretability. Through low-rank tensor factorization on a shared projection subspace, PolySAE captures pairwise and triple feature interactions with small parameter overhead (3% on GPT2). Across four language models and three SAE variants, PolySAE achieves an average improvement of approximately 8% in probing F1 while maintaining comparable reconstruction error, and produces 2-10$\times$ larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions. Critically, learned interaction weights exhibit negligible correlation with co-occurrence frequency ($r = 0.06$ vs. $r = 0.82$ for SAE feature covariance), suggesting that polynomial terms capture compositional structure, such as morphological binding and phrasal composition, largely independent of surface statistics.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features with Sparse Autoencoders without External Dataset Dependencies
papers.research_question: How does training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on out-of-distribution data affect their stability and feature faithfulness, and can training on the model's own synthetic data improve these aspects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FaithfulSAE, a method to train Sparse Autoencoders on the model's own synthetic data, which improves feature stability and reduces fake features compared to training on external datasets.
papers.conclusion: Training SAEs on the model's own synthetic data (FaithfulSAE) improves feature consistency and reduces fake features, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features.
papers.key_findings:
FaithfulSAEs trained on synthetic data show higher stability across seeds compared to SAEs trained on instruction datasets.
FaithfulSAEs achieve lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models compared to web-based dataset trained SAEs.
FaithfulSAEs outperform web-based SAEs in SAE probing tasks, indicating better reconstruction of the model's hidden state.
Shared Feature Ratio is higher when the target model and source model for synthetic data are the same, indicating that SAE training on its own data is more stable.
papers.limitation:
Lack of evaluation on instruction-tuned or reasoning models.
Shared Feature Ratio may not fully reflect the complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces.
Did not assess the interpretability of individual features through case studies.
future_direction: Exploring improved dataset generation and training strategies that could completely outperform Web-based methods.
Evaluating whether Faithful SAEs provide meaningful and interpretable explanations for individual features through detailed case studies.
Investigating the connection between pruning Fake Features and the principle of Minimal Description Length.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising solution for decomposing large language model representations into interpretable features. However, Paulo and Belrose (2025) have highlighted instability across different initialization seeds, and Heap et al. (2025) have pointed out that SAEs may not capture model-internal features. These problems likely stem from training SAEs on external datasets - either collected from the Web or generated by another model - which may contain out-of-distribution (OOD) data beyond the model's generalisation capabilities. This can result in hallucinated SAE features, which we term "Fake Features", that misrepresent the model's internal activations. To address these issues, we propose FaithfulSAE, a method that trains SAEs on the model's own synthetic dataset. Using FaithfulSAEs, we demonstrate that training SAEs on less-OOD instruction datasets results in SAEs being more stable across seeds. Notably, FaithfulSAEs outperform SAEs trained on web-based datasets in the SAE probing task and exhibit a lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models. Overall, our approach eliminates the dependency on external datasets, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features while highlighting the often neglected importance of SAE training datasets.

papers.title: Training Superior Sparse Autoencoders for Instruct Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on instruct models, given that existing methods designed for base models result in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Finetuning-aligned Sequential Training (FAST), a novel method for training sparse autoencoders on instruct models that aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns of instruct models, leading to significant improvements in reconstruction quality and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: FAST is an effective method for training SAEs on instruct models, achieving superior reconstruction and feature interpretability, and the resulting SAEs can be used to steer model behavior via special token features, opening new avenues for model control.
papers.key_findings:
FAST significantly outperforms baseline Block Training methods (BT(P) and BT(F)) in token reconstruction (MSE) and special token reconstruction (MSEst) across multiple instruct models and SAE architectures.
FAST produces a higher proportion of high-quality, interpretable features compared to baseline methods, as measured by an automated feature interpretability scoring framework.
Intervening on the activations of special tokens via the trained SAEs can improve output quality and enable fine-grained control of model behavior, suggesting new applications for SAEs.
future_direction: Exploring the opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior through steering with SAE latents, particularly via special tokens.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow in scale and capability, understanding their internal mechanisms becomes increasingly critical. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a key tool in mechanistic interpretability, enabling the extraction of human-interpretable features from LLMs. However, existing SAE training methods are primarily designed for base models, resulting in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability when applied to instruct models. To bridge this gap, we propose $\underline{\textbf{F}}$inetuning-$\underline{\textbf{a}}$ligned $\underline{\textbf{S}}$equential $\underline{\textbf{T}}$raining ($\textit{FAST}$), a novel training method specifically tailored for instruct models. $\textit{FAST}$ aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns characteristic of instruct models, resulting in substantial improvements in both reconstruction and feature interpretability. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, $\textit{FAST}$ achieves a mean squared error of 0.6468 in token reconstruction, significantly outperforming baseline methods with errors of 5.1985 and 1.5096. In feature interpretability, $\textit{FAST}$ yields a higher proportion of high-quality features, for Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, $21.1\%$ scored in the top range, compared to $7.0\%$ and $10.2\%$ for $\textit{BT(P)}$ and $\textit{BT(F)}$. Surprisingly, we discover that intervening on the activations of special tokens via the SAEs leads to improvements in output quality, suggesting new opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior. Code, data, and 240 trained SAEs are available at https://github.com/Geaming2002/FAST.

papers.title: Feature Extraction and Steering for Enhanced Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enhance the reasoning ability of LLMs without external datasets by extracting features from vanilla Chain-of-Thought and steering internal states?
papers.core_contribution: A framework that extracts reasoning features from vanilla CoT via verbal/symbolic decomposition and steers LLM activations to enhance reasoning without external datasets or retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature extraction and steering methods enhance reasoning in LLMs, and the SAE-free approach extends the benefits to models without corresponding SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based steering improves accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
SAE-free steering works without pre-trained SAEs and achieves comparable or better performance.
Steering increases reasoning length and attention to mathematical tokens.
There is an optimal steering strength; too high strength degrades performance.
The method suppresses noisy features and amplifies task-relevant reasoning features.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to mathematical reasoning datasets.
Experiments are limited to three model families (LLaMA, DeepSeek, Gemma).
future_direction: Extend to more diverse reasoning domains such as logical reasoning, scientific problem-solving, or multi-step planning.
Apply the method to more diverse LLM architectures to verify generalizability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate the ability to solve reasoning and mathematical problems using the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) technique. Expanding CoT length, as seen in models such as DeepSeek-R1, significantly enhances this reasoning for complex problems, but requires costly and high-quality long CoT data and fine-tuning. This work, inspired by the deep thinking paradigm of DeepSeek-R1, utilizes a steering technique to enhance the reasoning ability of an LLM without external datasets. Our method first employs Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract interpretable features from vanilla CoT. These features are then used to steer the LLM's internal states during generation. Recognizing that many LLMs do not have corresponding pre-trained SAEs, we further introduce a novel SAE-free steering algorithm, which directly computes steering directions from the residual activations of an LLM, obviating the need for an explicit SAE. Experimental results demonstrate that both our SAE-based and subsequent SAE-free steering algorithms significantly enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: TopK Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we build a language model architecture that enjoys the interpretability of sparse autoencoders without suffering the drawbacks of post-hoc training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TopK LMs, a transformer-based language model architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function to achieve inherent, SAE-like interpretability without requiring post-hoc training, while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: TopK LMs represent a significant advance toward trustworthy AI systems by making interpretability a built-in feature, demonstrating that performance and interpretability need not be competing objectives.
papers.key_findings:
TopK LMs achieve competitive language modeling and downstream task performance compared to dense baselines, with only a moderate increase in model size.
Neurons in TopK LMs exhibit higher concept specialization, as measured by lower token and semantic entropy, making them more interpretable.
Single-neuron interventions (activation patching) can causally steer the model's text generation towards specific concepts.
The formation and specialization of individual neurons can be traced continuously across training checkpoints and model layers.
Sparsity annealing during training improves convergence and model performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models up to ~1B parameters; effectiveness on significantly larger models remains an open question.
Evaluation focused on language modeling and standard reasoning benchmarks, leaving performance on specialized downstream tasks unclear.
Long-context modeling capabilities and the interaction between TopK sparsity and attention over long sequences were not examined.
The approach is currently limited to text-only models; extending to multimodal architectures requires future research.
Specific societal applications that could benefit from the model's interpretability were not explored.
future_direction: Scaling the TopK LM approach to significantly larger models (tens or hundreds of billions of parameters).
Extending TopK activation to multimodal architectures combining text with images, audio, or other modalities.
Investigating how TopK LMs can address concrete challenges in model alignment, fairness assessment, safety evaluation, and trustworthy AI deployment.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for analyzing and interpreting the activation space of transformer-based language models (LMs). However, SAEs suffer several shortcomings that diminish their utility and internal validity. Since SAEs are trained post-hoc, it is unclear if the failure to discover a particular concept is a failure on the SAE's side or due to the underlying LM not representing this concept. This problem is exacerbated by training conditions and architecture choices affecting which features an SAE learns. When tracing how LMs learn concepts during training, the lack of feature stability also makes it difficult to compare SAEs features across different checkpoints. To address these limitations, we introduce a modification to the transformer architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function at chosen layers, making the model's hidden states equivalent to the latent features of a TopK SAE. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc training while providing interpretability comparable to SAEs. The resulting TopK LMs offer a favorable trade-off between model size, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Despite this simple architectural change, TopK LMs maintain their original capabilities while providing robust interpretability benefits. Our experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations learned by TopK LMs enable successful steering through targeted neuron interventions and facilitate detailed analysis of neuron formation processes across checkpoints and layers. These features make TopK LMs stable and reliable tools for understanding how language models learn and represent concepts, which we believe will significantly advance future research on model interpretability and controllability.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
